# 106.208 — The finite Castelnuovo--Severi test for root correspondences

## 1. Purpose and stop criterion

Document 106.207 constructed two necessary pieces of a source
correspondence geometry:

* a hyperbolic plane generated by the polar rulings
  (F_{\mathrm v},F_{\mathrm h});
* genuine finite fiber products for the root covers
  (R_{Mn}\to R_M).

The hyperbolic plane is formal.  The next test must put an arithmetic
root graph inside it and decide whether its primitive part has the Hodge
sign.  For the graph \(\Gamma_n\), of bidegree \((1,n)\), the finite
Castelnuovo--Severi test is

\[
 \Gamma_n^2\leq 2n,
 \tag{1}
\]

or equivalently

\[
 \left(\Gamma_n-nF_{\mathrm v}-F_{\mathrm h}\right)^2\leq0.
 \tag{2}
\]

The stop rule is:

> The self-pairing must be obtained by finite incidence counting, with a
> cofinal normalization fixed independently of (1).  If its primitive
> value is positive, or if a sign has to be imposed, the source-geometry
> route stops.

The row-wise test passes strictly.  The result is not yet a global Hodge
index theorem, because intersections between different root surfaces
have not been constructed.

## 2. The finite incidence graph

For \(M,n\geq1\), let

\[
 R_M=\mathbb Z/M\mathbb Z,
 \qquad
 \pi_{Mn,M}:R_{Mn}\longrightarrow R_M
 \tag{3}
\]

be reduction modulo \(M\).  Its graph is

\[
 G_{M,n}
 =\{(a,a\bmod M):a\in R_{Mn}\}
 \subset R_{Mn}\times R_M.
 \tag{4}
\]

The first projection has degree one and the second has degree \(n\).
Thus

\[
 d_{\mathrm v}(G_{M,n})=1,
 \qquad
 d_{\mathrm h}(G_{M,n})=n.
 \tag{5}
\]

Let

\[
 U_n^{(M)}:\ell^2(R_M)\longrightarrow\ell^2(R_{Mn}),
 \qquad
 U_n^{(M)}f=f\circ\pi_{Mn,M}
 \tag{6}
\]

be the incidence matrix of (4).  Counting the \(n\) points in each
fiber gives

\[
 (U_n^{(M)})^*U_n^{(M)}=nI_M.
 \tag{7}
\]

### Definition 2.1 — Cofinal incidence self-pairing

Define

\[
 I_{M,n}(\Gamma_n,\Gamma_n)
 :=\frac1M\mathrm{Tr}
 \left((U_n^{(M)})^*U_n^{(M)}\right).
 \tag{8}
\]

The factor \(M^{-1}\) is not selected to force a sign.  It is the unique
cardinality normalization satisfying both

\[
 I_{M,1}(\Delta,\Delta)=1
 \tag{9}
\]

and invariance under uniform replication of the base root set.  In
particular, (8) is independent of the auxiliary level \(M\).

### Theorem 2.2 — Exact finite self-intersection

\[
 \boxed{I_{M,n}(\Gamma_n,\Gamma_n)=n.}
 \tag{10}
\]

#### Proof

Equation (7) gives

\[
 \frac1M\mathrm{Tr}(nI_M)=n.
\]

No limit or spectral datum is used. \(\square\)

The notation \(\Gamma_n^2=n\) below means the finite incidence
self-pairing (8).  It is a source-defined candidate for the diagonal
self-intersection.  A global intersection theory must still prove that
this incidence pairing is the correct Gysin self-intersection after the
finite and archimedean pages are joined.

## 3. Strict primitive negativity

Extend the row (10) by the polar intersections

\[
 F_{\mathrm v}^2=F_{\mathrm h}^2=0,
 \qquad
 F_{\mathrm v}F_{\mathrm h}=1,
 \tag{11}
\]

and by the projection degrees

\[
 \Gamma_nF_{\mathrm v}=1,
 \qquad
 \Gamma_nF_{\mathrm h}=n.
 \tag{12}
\]

The primitive projection is therefore

\[
 \Gamma_n^0
 =\Gamma_n-nF_{\mathrm v}-F_{\mathrm h}.
 \tag{13}
\]

It is orthogonal to both rulings.

### Theorem 3.1 — Finite Castelnuovo--Severi inequality

For every \(M,n\geq1\),

\[
 \boxed{
 \Gamma_n^2=n<2n
 =2d_{\mathrm v}(\Gamma_n)d_{\mathrm h}(\Gamma_n),}
 \tag{14}
\]

and

\[
 \boxed{(\Gamma_n^0)^2=-n<0.}
 \tag{15}
\]

#### Proof

Equation (14) follows from (5) and (10).  Expanding (13) with
(11)--(12) gives

\[
 \begin{aligned}
 (\Gamma_n^0)^2
 &=n-2n(\Gamma_nF_{\mathrm v})
      -2(\Gamma_nF_{\mathrm h})
      +2n(F_{\mathrm v}F_{\mathrm h})\\
 &=n-2n-2n+2n=-n.
 \end{aligned}
\]

Thus the negative sign is a consequence of finite fiber counting after
removing the two polar degrees; it is not postulated. \(\square\)

The intersection matrix on
\(\mathrm{span}\,\{F_{\mathrm v},F_{\mathrm h},\Gamma_n\}\) is

\[
 \begin{pmatrix}
 0&1&1\\
 1&0&n\\
 1&n&n
 \end{pmatrix},
 \tag{16}
\]

and has signature \((1,2)\).  Hence the arithmetic row has entered the
indefinite container in the correct primitive direction.

## 4. The square-root normalization is forced by the two degrees

Balance the graph by

\[
 \widehat\Gamma_n=n^{-1/2}\Gamma_n.
 \tag{17}
\]

Then

\[
 \widehat\Gamma_nF_{\mathrm v}=n^{-1/2},
 \qquad
 \widehat\Gamma_nF_{\mathrm h}=n^{1/2},
 \qquad
 \widehat\Gamma_n^2=1,
 \tag{18}
\]

and its primitive square is \(-1\).  Thus the midpoint coefficient
\(n^{-1/2}\) is not inserted independently: it is the smaller ruling
degree of the uniquely balanced graph.  For \(n=p^k\), multiplication by
the already proved relative root torsion \(\log p\) gives

\[
 (\log p)(\widehat\Gamma_{p^k}F_{\mathrm v})
 =\frac{\log p}{p^{k/2}}
 =\frac{\Lambda(p^k)}{\sqrt{p^k}}.
 \tag{19}
\]

This recovers the finite-place coefficient from one intersection row:
the square root comes from balancing the bidegree and the logarithm from
the relative determinant.

## 5. Transpose and the finite Rosati row

Transposition of (4) exchanges the two projections.  At the incidence
operator level it sends \(U_n^{(M)}\) to \((U_n^{(M)})^*\).  Therefore

\[
 (\Gamma_n^t\Gamma_n)_M=nI_M,
 \qquad
 \frac1M\mathrm{Tr}(\Gamma_n^t\Gamma_n)=n>0.
 \tag{20}
\]

The finite Rosati row and the primitive intersection row are consequently
the same count with opposite signs:

\[
 \boxed{
 \langle\Gamma_n,\Gamma_n\rangle_{\mathrm{Ros}}=n,
 \qquad
 (\Gamma_n^0)^2=-n.}
 \tag{21}
\]

This is the finite-root analogue of the passage from Rosati positivity to
negative definiteness on primitive divisor classes.

## 6. Composition and connected extraction are different products

The finite source now carries two operations that must not be identified.

1. **Categorical composition.** Fiber products give

   \[
    \Gamma_m\circ\Gamma_n=\Gamma_{mn}.
    \tag{22}
   \]

   This is the operation used by transpose and the Rosati row (20).

2. **Euler disjoint-union product.** The Hopf algebra records a connected
   return \(X_{p,k}\) and a disconnected product
   \(X_{p,1}X_{q,1}\) as different decorated objects.  The first
   Eulerian idempotent preserves the former and kills the latter.

After forgetting the decoration, both a connected composite cover and a
disconnected Euler product can have the same underlying integer degree.
Consequently the Eulerian idempotent does **not** descend to the collapsed
monoid \(\Gamma_m\circ\Gamma_n=\Gamma_{mn}\).  The factorization history
is required data.

This does not prevent a Rosati involution.  Transpose is defined on the
full correspondence category, while connected extraction is applied only
to the decorated orbit trace.  Naturality of the convolution logarithm
gives

\[
 \mathfrak e_1(X^t)=(\mathfrak e_1X)^t.
 \tag{23}
\]

What would fail is compressing categorical composition to the primitive
space.  Indeed, for primitive symbols \(X,Y\), generally

\[
 \mathfrak e_1(XY)=0
 \quad\text{while}\quad
 (\mathfrak e_1X)(\mathfrak e_1Y)=XY.
 \tag{24}
\]

Thus the connected space is not an algebra and must not be used as the
domain of Rosati multiplication.  A global construction must retain the
full decorated correspondence category, perform transpose and
composition there, and apply \(\mathfrak e_1\) only at the cyclic trace.

## 7. Strength and limitation of the test

The test passes more strongly than mere positivity:

* the self-pairing is the normalized cardinality of a genuine finite
  graph;
* the primitive square is strictly negative and equals \(-n\);
* the balanced ruling coefficient is exactly \(n^{-1/2}\);
* relative torsion then produces the literal von Mangoldt coefficient;
* transpose gives a positive finite Rosati row without using a zero.

But (14) is still a **single-row** theorem.  It does not prove a Hodge
index inequality for linear combinations of different prime-power rows.
Those rows initially live on different products
\(R_{Mp^k}\times R_M\), and no source-defined cross-intersection
\(\Gamma_m\Gamma_n\) on one common degree-two page has yet been supplied.
The possible negative index of the global cross matrix is therefore not
decided by (15).

The exact next falsifier is now sharper:

> Construct the common-refinement cross-pairing
> (I(\Gamma_m,\Gamma_n)\) from finite fiber products, including the
> factorization decoration, and test whether the primitive Gram matrix is
> negative semidefinite for every finite collection of root rows.

If that matrix acquires a positive primitive eigenvalue, the geometric
route stops before the Gamma fiber is attached.  If it remains negative,
the finite arithmetic Hodge block has been constructed and can then be
joined to the archimedean boundary.

## 8. Status

Proved from finite root combinatorics:

* \(\Gamma_n^2=n\) under the cofinally normalized incidence pairing;
* the strict row-wise Castelnuovo--Severi inequality
  \(\Gamma_n^2<2d_{\mathrm v}d_{\mathrm h}\);
* the exact primitive value \((\Gamma_n^0)^2=-n\);
* the structural origin of \(p^{-k/2}\) from balanced bidegree;
* the positive transpose/Rosati row;
* the necessity of keeping categorical composition distinct from the
  Euler disjoint-union product.

Still open:

* the common-refinement cross-intersection matrix;
* its Hodge sign for arbitrary finite linear combinations;
* the subsequent Gamma--polar gluing and global diagonal trace.
